extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and writing students (novice to intermediate) learning how to handle exposition and description in scenes and dialogue
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for using dialogue, description, symbols, and scene construction to convey exposition without resorting to clumsy info-dumps. Focuses on how to make exposition serve plot, character, and conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'as you know, Bob' / maid-and-butler dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: 'As you know, Bob…' is the trope-tastic line we use to refer to expository dialog which has no function beyond exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write scenes in which two characters tell each other information they both already know solely to inform the reader. Anti-pattern example: forensic scientists reciting textbook facts to each other (CSI Miami). If exposition lacks an in-scene reason (conflict, disbelief, ignorance), cut or rework it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer dialogue to infodump but make it feel natural
rubrics_metrics.description: First level: dialogue is more fun to read than a big infodump. Second level: realize the dialogue must feel natural, not like exposition dummies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialogue instead of large blocks of narrator explanation, but construct dialogue so it sounds like real people speaking and not like lines written only to convey facts. Test lines for naturalness and character voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure scenes have plot movement beyond dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only forward movement in the scene is through the dialogue, then your scene is not working as a holistic scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate verbal content from the plot purpose of the scene. Ask: what else is this scene accomplishing (plot advancement, decision, reversal)? Add physical context or actions that move the plot as well as the conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie exposition to conflict and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything that you learn, be it dialogue or exposition, should be tied to conflict and character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor exposition to what characters want, believe, or dispute. Make the imparting of information a moment of disagreement, persuasion, or character revelation so it carries dramatic weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbols and visible actions to communicate information
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign a visible thing or an action to a thing (symbol) to convey information without explicit statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Luke turning off his targeting computer to show growth; Toy Story repeating a birthday-scene motif to show change in Woody. Use visual motifs or repeated actions so the reader infers meaning instead of being told it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build dialogue outward from the point
rubrics_metrics.description: When you write dialogue, build outward from the point — what the participants are trying to get to — instead of starting at hello and proceeding linearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the goal of the conversation and craft lines that move toward that goal; skip irrelevant preliminaries. This keeps dialogue focused and purposeful rather than meandering exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: All conversation should have conflict (conversation-as-combat)
rubrics_metrics.description: All conversation is combat; there should be competing ideas or stakes so the conversation changes something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there's no conflict or reason for the characters to convey/receive information, rework the scene. Even agreement can contain tension (belief vs. disbelief, status shifts), which makes exposition engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an ignorant/late-arriving character to fast-track exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a person enter the conversation late who doesn't know what's been discussed lets you deliver exposition naturally with conflict and comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A latecomer provides a believable in-scene reason for other characters to recap information. Use their ignorance to create friction or status dynamics while informing the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using action beats on every line of dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-pattern: every line of dialogue is modified by a sentence saying what the speaker is doing (slamming cup, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't use an action on each line as a crutch to 'fix' weak dialogue. Instead, create a bracketing paragraph(s) of scene motion around blocks of dialogue, or use sparse, meaningful beats to punctuate rather than annotate every line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create blocks: scene bracketing separate from dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Work in a block of the scene (context/motion) and then a block of dialogue, rather than slicing descriptive beats between every line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bracketing the dialogue with context paragraphs is often more efficient and readable than inserting micro-beats continuously. It preserves flow and allows dialogue to carry emotion with less interruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only tell the reader what they need to know
rubrics_metrics.description: Only tell the reader what they need to know, and pace the learning curve of worldbuilding elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the essential worldbuilding elements for your story and study how other media introduce them; reveal details gradually and only as they matter to the scene or reader understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pare descriptive prose: write five sentences then reduce
rubrics_metrics.description: Write five sentences, then pare it down. Ask if one sentence will do the same amount of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compress paragraphs to one or two powerful sentences whenever possible. Overwriting is acceptable in drafting, but in revision aim for pointed, high-weight sentences that pull their own weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emulate screenwriting/comic techniques for scene-mood description
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the scene with just enough for a director or artist: establish mood, colors, and spatial relationships rather than cataloging every detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think in terms of shots (establishing shot, foreground/background, desaturation) and translate that into prose (mention nearest tree, feel of vast space, a key color) to create mood without exhaustive lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spatial intimacy / iceberg approach to worldbuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot paint an entire city; paint one room or one street and let the reader infer the rest (one curtain open vs. handing a key to the whole house).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a few evocative details that imply the larger world. Those details should be carefully chosen to reflect themes, character, or story so the reader can infer the rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie descriptive details to character attention and perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Each character notices different things; tie the details you give to what the POV character would actually perceive and care about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a character's biases, profession, and goals to filter description. This prevents omniscient info-dumps and makes exposition feel anchored and character-driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make exposition pointed and purposeful
rubrics_metrics.description: The pointedness of exposition is important: exposition should serve a purpose in the scene and be specific to the characters involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generic worldbuilding paragraphs that don't intersect with character or plot. Ensure each piece of exposition has an in-scene reason (stakes, disbelief, decision) or else cut it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition of scenes/motifs to show change rather than state facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reusing a scene or motif (e.g., Toy Story’s birthday-scene echoed later) can demonstrate character growth or world change without explicit commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan structural echoes or visual callbacks that let readers see the arc rather than being told it; repetition with variation implies development and avoids overt exposition.
